subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The Norman Conquest & Control
subtitle: How William the Conqueror seized England in 1066 and enforced Norman rule.

data.targetWord: the process of deciding who becomes the next ruler after a monarch dies

examples.en-GB: Edward the Confessor's death caused a succession crisis because he had no direct heir.

data.targetWord: a person who declares they have a right to a throne or title

examples.en-GB: William of Normandy was a claimant to the English throne in 1066.

data.targetWord: a council of important Anglo-Saxon nobles and churchmen who advised the king and helped choose the next ruler

examples.en-GB: The Witan chose Harold Godwinson as king after Edward the Confessor died.

data.targetWord: professional soldiers who served Anglo-Saxon kings and nobles as a permanent fighting force

examples.en-GB: Harold's housecarls formed the core of the English shield wall at Hastings.

data.targetWord: part-time soldiers raised from local communities in Anglo-Saxon England to defend against attack

examples.en-GB: Harold called up the fyrd to fight the Viking invasion in the north.

data.targetWord: a military tactic where soldiers pretend to run away in order to draw the enemy out of a defensive formation

examples.en-GB: The Norman cavalry used a feigned retreat to lure English soldiers off Senlac Hill.

data.targetWord: a defensive battle formation where soldiers stand side by side with overlapping shields to create a solid barrier

examples.en-GB: The English shield wall on Senlac Hill held firm for much of the battle.

data.targetWord: an early Norman castle design consisting of a raised earthen mound called a motte with a wooden tower, next to an enclosed courtyard called a bailey

examples.en-GB: William ordered motte-and-bailey castles to be built quickly across England to control rebellions.

data.targetWord: a way of organising society around land and loyalty, where the king granted land to nobles who provided military service, and peasants farmed the land

examples.en-GB: The feudal system helped William reward loyal Normans with English land.

data.targetWord: a powerful lord who held land directly from the king and owed him military service and loyalty

examples.en-GB: Norman tenants-in-chief received large estates and were expected to provide knights for the king.

data.targetWord: a detailed survey of land, resources and wealth in England ordered by William I in 1085 and completed in 1086, used to calculate tax and settle land disputes

examples.en-GB: The Domesday Book shows that many Anglo-Saxon landowners had been replaced by Norman lords.

data.targetWord: William's brutal campaign of destruction across parts of northern England in 1069 to 1070, intended to crush rebellion by destroying food, homes and livelihoods

examples.en-GB: The Harrying of the North caused widespread famine and depopulation in the north of England.

data.targetWord: an organised attempt by a group to resist or overthrow those in authority

examples.en-GB: Several rebellions broke out in England after 1066 as people resisted Norman rule.

data.targetWord: a moment or event that causes significant and lasting change in the course of history

examples.en-GB: Historians often describe 1066 as a major turning point in English history.

data.targetWord: aspects of life or society that remain the same over time despite other changes occurring around them

examples.en-GB: Continuity after 1066 included village farming, Christianity and local administration.

data.targetWord: soldiers who fight on horseback, used in medieval warfare to charge enemy lines and pursue retreating forces

examples.en-GB: Norman cavalry played a key role in breaking the English shield wall at Hastings.

data.targetWord: a strong stone tower forming the main defensive building of a castle, replacing earlier wooden structures to provide more permanent and impressive fortification

examples.en-GB: The White Tower in London is an example of a stone keep built by the Normans.

data.targetWord: the act of taking control of a territory or people by military force

examples.en-GB: The Norman Conquest transformed English landholding, government and culture.

data.targetWord: a powerful Anglo-Saxon noble who governed a large region of England on behalf of the king

examples.en-GB: Harold Godwinson was Earl of Wessex, the most powerful earldom in England.

data.targetWord: a historian's explanation of why events happened or what they meant, which may differ from other historians' views based on evidence used

examples.en-GB: Different interpretations of Hastings disagree about whether luck or tactics were most important.

data.targetWord: a trained mounted warrior who owed military service to a lord in exchange for a grant of land

examples.en-GB: Knights were expected to fight for their lord when called upon.

data.targetWord: a rural worker who farmed the land, often with limited freedom, and owed labour, rent or produce to a lord

examples.en-GB: Most peasants continued to farm the same land after 1066, though their lords changed.

data.targetWord: a duchy in northern France ruled by William before 1066, which shaped his claim to the English throne and his style of governance

examples.en-GB: William used his experience as Duke of Normandy to organise his invasion fleet.

data.targetWord: the ridge near Hastings where Harold positioned his English army and fought the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066

examples.en-GB: Harold's army held Senlac Hill defensively while William's forces attacked from below.

data.targetWord: information about who created a historical source, when, why and for whom, used to assess its reliability and usefulness

examples.en-GB: The provenance of the Bayeux Tapestry suggests it presents a Norman perspective on 1066.

data.title: Key events of 1066 in order
items: Edward the Confessor dies in January
Harold Godwinson is crowned King Harold II
Harald Hardrada invades the north; Battle of Fulford
Harold defeats Hardrada at Stamford Bridge
William lands at Pevensey in the south
William defeats Harold at the Battle of Hastings
William is crowned King of England at Westminster

data.title: Norman methods of control after 1066 — from quickest to most long-lasting
items: Build motte-and-bailey castles to control towns and roads
Redistribute land to loyal Norman followers
Use the feudal system to link land to military service
Crush rebellions, including the Harrying of the North
Commission the Domesday survey to record land and tax

data.title: Stages of the Battle of Hastings
items: English army takes up position on Senlac Hill in shield wall
Norman archers fire at the English line
Norman infantry and cavalry attack uphill
Some English soldiers break formation chasing a Norman retreat
Normans exploit the gap and attack the weakened shield wall
Harold is killed and the English army collapses

data.title: Changes and continuities after 1066 — sort each into the correct group

pairs.text: Land ownership passed to Norman lords
Norman French became important in law and government
Many Norman bishops replaced Anglo-Saxon church leaders
Most people continued to farm the same fields
The system of shires and sheriffs continued
Local taxation systems continued under Norman control
